doc.title: Ignacio Berroa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 24, 2021 [interview 1 of 2]

title: What Dizzy asked of his drummers
summary: Dizzy wanted a particular ride cymbal feel and taught fills in the gaps and bebop vocabulary.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: You know talking about music between musicians I find fascinating because usually if I ask the question of some performing musicians do you all talk about what you’re going to do or do you talk after you’re done? And most of them say not really, that it happens on the bandstand. So I wonder if Dizzy Gillespie talked to you about what he wanted?

Oh yes. Oh yes. Yes. Dizzy was famous for being a pain in the neck for drummers. Especially for drummers. And yes, he wanted to hear certain things in particular like for example Dizzy was not too keen or he didn’t like playing the cymbal behind him like let’s say in a modern way of playing it. He didn’t like moving that straight ahead pulse, playing around. He wanted to hear [scats]. He was not too keen about [scats]. That type of thing, he would always say to me, “Ignacio, behind me you play [scats]. Behind Sam Rivers and behind Ed Cherry the guitar — , you play whatever you want. But behind me I want to hear — every drummer that went through that band had that famous 22 Chinese cymbal with rivets, that was the sound he liked to hear when he played. You had to play on that cymbal and he would ask you to play that. And also he taught me a great deal of the bebop vocabulary that a lot of the young musicians call “rules” because I want to be

me, I have to play like me and so forth and so on. Vocabulary. He taught me a great deal about the vocabulary, how to fill the holes. When he would play a phrase, a phrase, and then filling when he was gasping for air [scats]. That’s where you play your fill. You know?
Yeah. Don’t play over his lick, play in the cracks.

Exactly. Exactly. While he’s playing you can be complementing, very soft you know, and underneath on the underground, but not competing with him. Then when the soloist gasps for air, that’s the moment where you can play your fills. That’s part of the vocabulary. That’s part of the vocabulary, things that should be learned. And I learned that very well. That was the type of thing he taught me. We talked about rhythms, we talked about fusion rhythms, he was — at some point he was with me, I was like his rhythm machine. We would be on the stage and Dizzy would think about a rhythm, he will come to the drum, whisper the rhythm in my ear, and I would play it back to him. So we were always having that type of communication. But yeah, he was — the thing he was very demanding like all the band leaders, he also was demanding about the type of chord he wanted to hear while he was improvising. Dizzy Gillespie was like, I tell people, being with Dizzy Gillespie was like being at a university of jazz. But yes, he was demanding. Most of the band leaders that I remember back in the days they were very demanding. They knew what they wanted to hear and so forth and so on. And I think that was very good.
